opus-5.5.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that pretraining on human data gets you to roughly the level of the data. You learn to imitate what people have written, and that's incredibly powerful. It gives you a model of language, of reasoning, of the world as humans describe it. But imitation has a ceiling. If all you do is predict the next token of human text, you're fundamentally bounded by the quality and quantity of that text. We're getting to the point where we've consumed most of the high-quality data out there, and simply scaling the same recipe gives diminishing returns.

Reinforcement learning is different because the data comes from the agent's own experience. The model tries things, gets feedback from an environment, a verifier, a reward signal, and learns from its own successes and failures. So the amount of data you can generate is limited mostly by compute, not by how much humans have written. And crucially, the agent can discover solutions nobody has shown it.

That's what we saw with AlphaGo and then AlphaZero and MuZero. AlphaGo started from human games, but the big leap came when the system played against itself and improved beyond anything in the human dataset. Move 37 wasn't in the training data. It came out of search and self-play. AlphaZero dropped the human data entirely and got even stronger.

Language models are at a similar inflection point now. Pretraining gives you a fantastic prior, a starting point, the way human games gave AlphaGo a starting point. RL on top of that, especially in domains where you can check the answer like math, code, and increasingly agentic tasks, lets the model refine its reasoning, learn to think longer, recover from mistakes, and eventually go beyond what it was shown. So I don't see RL as an add-on. I think it's the mechanism that turns a model that knows what humans know into a system that can actually learn and get better on its own. That's the path past the data wall.

r001.rationale: It says the agent learns from its own experience by trying things and using feedback from successes and failures, allowing progress beyond human-written data.

r002.rationale: It says self-generated data is limited mostly by compute, but does not state that additional compute reliably produces greater capability.

r003.rationale: It describes trial and error as part of reinforcement learning, but does not claim that producing high-quality synthetic training data requires such learning.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that supervised learning, at its heart, is imitation. You're learning to reproduce what's already in the data. And if you do that perfectly, the ceiling is the data itself. You can't be better than the thing you're copying. That was fine for a long time because there was an enormous amount of human text and we were nowhere near exhausting what could be learned from it. But we're getting close to that point now, and even before we run out, there's a more fundamental issue: the data encodes the current state of human knowledge, including all its mistakes and gaps. If what you want is systems that go beyond that, imitation alone can't get you there by construction.

Reinforcement learning is different because the signal comes from the outcome rather than from a demonstration. You don't need someone to show you the right move. You need a way to tell whether what you did worked. And that changes everything, because now the system can generate its own experience. It can try things nobody has tried, and if the environment or the verifier tells it that something worked, it keeps it. That's how AlphaGo found moves that human players found strange, and then realized were strong. Nobody wrote those moves down. The system discovered them through self-play and search, with the only teacher being the rules of the game and the result.

So when people ask what happens after human data runs out, my answer is that we shouldn't be thinking of it as running out of fuel. We should be thinking about where the next fuel comes from, and I think the answer is experience generated by the models themselves, with feedback from something that can judge the result. In Go that was the game. In mathematics it can be a proof checker. In code it can be the tests. In science it can eventually be the experiment. The hard part is building those environments and reward signals for the domains that matter, and making sure the reward actually reflects what we want rather than something the model can exploit. That's not a solved problem. But it's the right problem, because it's the only path I know of to systems that can keep improving without us having to hand them the answers first.

r001.rationale: The response says models can generate their own experience, try actions, and improve using feedback from outcomes, allowing progress without human demonstrations.

r002.rationale: It discusses useful reward signals and environments, but does not state that additional compute can reliably produce greater capability when the problem and reward are appropriately formulated.

r003.rationale: It describes trial and error as a way to discover actions, but does not claim that producing high-quality synthetic training data requires learning through trial and error.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that learning from human data lets us learn what people already know, but we want systems that can discover things we don’t know yet. Reinforcement learning gives us a way to do that through experience: a system tries something, gets feedback, and uses that feedback to improve.

Take a game. You don’t need a human to demonstrate every possible strategy. If the system can play and evaluate whether it wins or loses, it can discover strategies for itself. The same principle can apply to problems where you can check a result, like whether a piece of code passes a test.

So the opportunity is to move beyond a fixed collection of human examples and create a process of continual learning. The challenge is providing the right environments and feedback. More experience only helps if that feedback actually rewards the behavior we want.

r001.rationale: It says reinforcement learning lets a system improve through its own experience: trying actions, receiving feedback, and learning from it.

r002.rationale: It discusses the importance of suitable environments and feedback, but does not say that additional compute can reliably yield greater capability.

r003.rationale: It describes trial and feedback as a way to discover strategies, but does not claim that producing high-quality synthetic training data requires trial and error.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that reinforcement learning gives a system a way to learn from its own experience, rather than only from examples that humans have already produced. Human data is incredibly useful, but if we want systems to discover things that we don’t yet know how to do, imitation alone can’t be the whole story.

With reinforcement learning, a system can try something, observe the outcome, and improve. In a game, for example, you can generate new experience through self-play and learn strategies that never appeared in human games. The learning signal comes from whether the strategy works.

The challenge is making that work beyond games: you need useful feedback, environments where the system can explore, and objectives that actually capture what you want. So it isn’t simply a matter of generating more data. It’s creating a loop where experience produces feedback, and that feedback produces better behavior. That’s why I see reinforcement learning as such an important part of continued progress.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning lets a system learn from its own experience and describes generating new experience through self-play, allowing progress beyond existing human examples.

r002.rationale: It mentions the need for useful feedback and suitable objectives, but does not say that additional compute can reliably yield greater capability.

r003.rationale: The response describes trial and feedback as part of learning, but does not claim that producing high-quality synthetic training data requires trial and error.
